newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Howard fails to settle Aborigine land row.
newsitem.headline: Howard fails to settle Aborigine land row.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Monday failed to reach an agreement with Aborigines over native land title, saying he needed more time to discuss the contentious issue with indigenous leaders.

Prior to meeting Aboriginal leaders on Monday, Howard said he would present his government's position and hoped he was close to a settlement on the issue, which Australian farmers say is damaging their industry.
"Considerable progress has been achieved," Howard said in a statement after the meeting. "However, several important issues require more discussion."

Aboriginal leaders emerged from the meeting saying they had agreed on some issues but failed to make progress on issues such as the rights of Aborigines to negotiate development of land on which they had native-title interest.

Aborigines last Friday threatened to seek U.N. trade sanctions against Australia if the government extinguished native title as argued by farmers and conservative rural politicians, including the Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer.
Howard, rejecting the call to simply extinguish native title, has been negotiating with both sides but has warned that if they can't reach agreement he will impose a solution.
Newspapers reported on Monday that a key element of Howard's plan would be to abolish any native title rights that were inconsistent with farmers carrying on pastoral activities.
But the plan would also guarantee access rights to the land for Aborigines. "What I've put forward does not involve blanket extinguishment," Howard said, describing his plan.
Howard said a government task force would now examine the issues raised in Monday's talks and he would discuss the results with Aboriginal leaders on Thursday.
"Also I propose to call an early meeting of state premiers and chief ministers to discuss the whole matter," he said.
The High Court of Australia in 1992 ruled that native title existed in Australia, overturning the old assumption a Terra Nullius or empty land when British settlers arrived in 1788.

The ruling set off a prolonged and bitter dispute in which the former Labor government looked for a way of regulating native title and limiting any economic damage from it without discriminating against Aborigines.
In 1993 the then Labor government introduced native title laws covering Crown land, but not pastoral land.
But in December 1996 the High Court ruled that Aborigines had unspecified native title rights to land that the government had leased to pastoralists.
Howard has said that 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) of land was "potentially claimable" by Aborigines under native title laws.
